w: A narrow zig-zag tunnel cut into living rock leads to a chamber lined with niches -- one held mummies, another a silver plate angled to throw sunlight across the room. Bones piled in the stone gutter outside point to ritual sacrifice, not just prayer. Quechua for 'zig-zag,' and it still forces a stoop to pass through.

w: Its walls glow red at dusk -- hence the Quechua name, 'red fortress' -- and the effect isn't decoration. Puka Pukara's terraces, staircases and thick defensive walls formed part of the ring guarding Inca Cusco, doubling as an administrative post on the road out of the capital. A working fort dressed as a sunset.
s: Red-walled Inca fort guarding the road to Cusco
_facts: name means red fortress in Quechua

w: Boulders the size of vans, cut and fitted without mortar so tightly a blade won't slide between them -- Inca chroniclers credited the citadel to Pachacuti and his successors. It sits above Cusco at nearly 3,700 metres, and in 1983 UNESCO listed it alongside the city itself. Nothing here has moved in five centuries.

designated UNESCO World Heritage Site with Cusco in 1983

w: A round tower with triple concentric walls, once aligned to the zenith sunrise -- and, in 1536, the site of one soldier's last stand. As Sacsayhuaman fell to the Spanish, the warrior Cahuide is said to have leapt from its summit rather than surrender. The tower was dismantled soon after; only its foundations remain.

temple and towers dismantled during Spanish rule

w: Spanish builders raised their Dominican monastery directly onto the walls of the Coricancha, the Inca Empire's holiest temple -- leaving the Inca stonework standing beneath their own Baroque arches. The complex fuses both eras: a church, two cloisters, original Inca masonry, and a working museum of Inca artifacts.

w: Jesuits built their church directly over an Inca palace on the Plaza de Armas, and its facade became a template for Baroque architecture across the southern Andes. Begun in 1576, wrecked by the 1650 earthquake, rebuilt by 1673 -- twice-built, and still one of the finest Spanish Baroque interiors in Peru.

built on an Inca palace
one of the best examples of Spanish Baroque architecture in Peru
construction began 1576, damaged in 1650 earthquake, rebuilt by 1673
influenced Baroque architecture development in the South Andes

w: 'Little Cuzco' perches at 3,650 metres above the Sacred Valley, a royal estate likely built around 1420 by the Inca emperor Viracocha. Its Inca-era name, Kakya Qawani, was all but forgotten until 20th-century archaeologists renamed it -- three kilometres and 730 metres of elevation above the town of Lamay below.

w: Once a swamp drained by the Incas into the empire's ceremonial heart, then Cusco's central stage since the Spanish refounding in 1534 -- this square has watched victories celebrated and rebels executed, including Tupac Amaru II in 1781. Colonial cathedrals now ring the plaza where Inca palaces once stood.

w: Roughly 450 pieces drawn from Peru's Larco Museum collection sit inside Cusco's San Blas district -- gold, ceramics and textiles spanning pre-Columbian cultures from across the country, not just the Inca. A small, quiet counterpoint to the ruins outside, and a crash course in everything that came before them.

w: A natural lookout over Cusco at 3,600 metres, its Quechua name simply means 'red hill' -- but the summit is now better known for the white statue standing on it, Cristo Blanco, watching over the old Inca capital below. Come for the panorama over the historic centre; the Christ figure is the bonus.

_facts: name is Quechua for red hill

w: Terraced fields, watchtowers, guard posts and a ceremonial centre run the length of a mountain ridge above the market town of Pisac -- a full working Inca settlement, not just a single ruin. Declared a national archaeological park in 1983, it protects one of the Sacred Valley's largest Inca complexes.

w: One of the most revered wak'as -- sacred sites -- of the entire Inca world, this 4,089-metre peak southeast of Cusco carries a name recorded in half a dozen spellings across the chronicles. Sacred peaks like this one anchored Inca cosmology long before Machu Picchu made headlines.

w: Fourteen stone terraces cling to a hillside above the Urubamba River near Chinchero, a Quechua name that just means 'old storehouse' -- likely all this site ever was, a working Inca deposit rather than a palace. These days the ruins share their hillside with craft stalls and, incongruously, a zip line.
